common_name: Aji Chombo Pepper (Panamanian Scotch Bonnet-Type Chile)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since chinense types germinate slowly and need sustained warmth.

directions: Aji Chombo is Panama's everyday Scotch Bonnet-type chile, the signature heat behind the country's bottled hot sauces and pickled vegetable condiments. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with warm soil, since germination is slow and uneven at cool temperatures, then transplant into a sunny bed only once nights stay reliably above 60F. The compact, bushy plants bear small, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through yellow to orange-red, carrying classic fruity, citrusy chinense aroma alongside intense heat. Harvest continually with gloved hands to keep plants setting new flowers through the long warm season.
sources: general horticultural reference on Panamanian aji chombo

common_name: Peach Ghost Scorpion Pepper (Ghost x Trinidad Scorpion Natural Cross)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this superhot is slow to germinate and needs the longest warm season possible.

directions: Peach Ghost Scorpion (also called Jay's Peach Ghost Scorpion) is a naturally occurring open-pollinated cross between ghost pepper (bhut jolokia) and Trinidad Scorpion lines, discovered by grower Jay Weaver in a Pennsylvania ghost-pepper field and later stabilized from saved seed, selected for pale peach-orange, gnarled, scorpion-tailed pods instead of the red or chocolate tones typical of similar hybrids. Start seed early and keep soil consistently warm, since chinense superhots stall in cool conditions and this slow-ripening type needs every extra week of a long growing season to color up fully. Stake plants once the heavy fruit clusters develop, and keep moisture even, since inconsistent watering triggers blossom drop. Handle ripe pods with gloves and eye protection, as the heat is well into superhot territory with persistent oleoresin transfer.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Melanzana Rossa di Rotonda Scarlet Eggplant (Italian DOP Tomato-Shaped Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 8 weeks before transplanting; this Italian heirloom DOP crop from Rotonda, Basilicata ripens to an intense red and benefits from a full, hot summer season.

directions: Melanzana Rossa di Rotonda is a scarlet eggplant (Solanum aethiopicum) grown under Italy's DOP protected-origin designation around the town of Rotonda in Basilicata, ripening to an intense red with a ribbed, rounded shape closely resembling a large tomato rather than a typical eggplant. Start seed indoors with warm soil and transplant only after the weather is reliably warm, since this type needs a long season to fully color. The dense, meaty flesh is traditionally harvested at the red stage and is prized in southern Italian cooking for stuffing, grilling, and preserving in oil. Stake plants as the fruit load builds, and pick regularly to encourage continued set through the season.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity - Melanzana Rossa di Rotonda

common_name: Mattu Gulla Eggplant (Udupi GI-Tagged Indian Heirloom Round Green Brinjal)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Mattu Gulla is traditionally grown in the sandy coastal soils of Udupi, India, and appreciates loose, well-drained beds.

directions: Mattu Gulla is a round green eggplant, grown traditionally on the sandy coastal fields of Mattu village near Udupi in Karnataka, India, where it holds a Geographical Indication tag tying it to that specific growing region; it is notably green rather than purple, distinguishing it from most other brinjal grown nearby. Start seed indoors in warm soil and transplant into loose, sandy, well-drained beds once nights are reliably warm, since this type is adapted to lean coastal soil rather than rich garden loam. The fruit is prized in Udupi's temple-associated cuisine for its mild, slightly sweet flavor and tender flesh, most famously in the regional Mattu Gulla curry. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and firm, and pick regularly to keep the compact plants productive through the season.
sources: Geographical Indications Registry of India - Mattu Gulla
